The man had heard that Chase was the guy building a new data center in town—and he wanted to say: Please don’t. “He had a beautiful home that he paid for and had been living in for years, and was concerned that his view would be disrupted,” Chase told me. It is where the election of 2026 took place, spiritually and politically. It is where the governing strategy for the Democratic Party should now reside. The midterm election really began in Minnesota during the winter ICE raids and the brutal deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The question nagged throughout the year: Is this who we are? Didn’t a guy like Pretti treat me at the hospital when I slashed my hand on the job? Didn’t we all know a wandering soul like Good, who had landed in Minneapolis with her three kids just eight months earlier? It was the subtext for all that followed. We wanted the border closed—good job, Mr. President—but did we really vote for brutal, masked gangster feds fighting our fellow citizens in the streets? Read more

articles.title: The End of the Trump Era
articles.author: Eugene Robinson
articles.summary: Well, that was weird. The Donald Trump era, I mean. It’s over now. It ended yesterday when voters handed control of both houses of Congress to the Democratic Party, along with a clear set of instructions: Stop the madness. Be honest. Be competent. Be normal. Be nice. Trump will still be president for another two years, of course, and it is unimaginable that he will go gently into lame-duck irrelevance. But the Republican Party, or what is left of it, surely must realize that the late Senator Lindsey Graham from South Carolina was right—though a decade premature—when in 2016 he warned : “If we nominate Trump we will get destroyed.......and we will deserve it.” Graham’s Senate seat will be occupied for the next six years by the pediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat. The last time a Democrat held that seat was in 1964, just before Strom Thurmond changed parties and became a Republican. Trump’s handpicked GOP candidate—Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister—lost by coming across to voters as utterly clueless. articles.summary: On the eve of an election that threatened to upend his presidency, Donald Trump went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he had overseen a multimillion-dollar renovation that went awry when its new coating peeled and algae turned the water green. Aides hoped the President would focus on the concerns weighing on ordinary Americans: soaring gas prices, expensive groceries, a new war in the Middle East. Instead, Trump spent much of his 53-minute speech talking about construction projects rather than the struggles of the nation he had been elected to serve. It was a bewildering capstone to a strange campaign. Allies marveled at Trump’s inability to stay on message as he crisscrossed the country. articles.summary: Senator-elect Troy Jackson in Portland, Maine on Nov. 4, 2026. —ophie Park/Bloomberg—Getty Images We counted, and this midterm election cycle, there were just seven major-party candidates for Congress who had working-class jobs when they first got into politics. The last ballots are still being totaled, but many of the politicians from working-class backgrounds who ran won, or seem poised to win. During national elections, we often hear a lot about the rare candidates who had working-class jobs. If you follow politics, you’re likely to know that Maine’s newly elected Senator Troy Jackson was a logger, or that New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was a bartender. But these candidates are the exceptions to an often-unspoken rule of U.S. politics: the working class doesn’t govern. Our research shows that people in working-class positions—manual labor jobs like construction worker, service industry jobs like restaurant server, and clerical jobs like receptionist—almost never go on to hold elected office. articles.author: By Alex Gangitano, Sophia Cai and Lisa Kashinsky
articles.summary: Joe Biden was unceremoniously ushered out of the White House two years ago. On Tuesday, he got a small measure of revenge. Prominent Biden administration alumni are winning in a handful of notable races, with Keisha Lance Bottoms — the one-time Atlanta mayor turned Biden’s senior adviser and director of the Office of Public Engagement — leading the pack by flipping Georgia’s governorship.
